clue.text: Re-invest till sponsor appears

parts.note: to till land is to plough it
to sponsor someone is to back them

explanation.surface: Someone puts money back into a business once a backer turns up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Till' looks like the cash drawer or 'until', but here it is the farming verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To plough back profits is to put them back into the business, i.e. reinvest them.

clue.text: Soldier taken to embrace Resistance Front

indicators.note: to embrace means to hold inside, so one piece surrounds the other

parts.note: a soldier taken in war is a POW, a prisoner of war
R is the physics symbol for resistance

explanation.surface: A captured soldier hugs a leader of the Resistance movement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Resistance Front' reads as a partisan movement; 'Front' is in fact the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The prow is the front end of a ship, so front defines it.

clue.text: Poet who knew Donne and Jonson latterly

indicators.note: latterly suggests the end, so take the final letter of each word

explanation.surface: A poet who was acquainted with the poets Donne and Ben Jonson in later life.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue implies a contemporary of Donne, but the poet is the First World War poet Wilfred Owen.
explanation.definitionFit: Wilfred Owen was an English war poet, so he is an example of a poet.

clue.text: Grapevine cultivator's second new press going outside

indicators.note: the rearranged letters go outside, around, the abbreviation for second
new means remade, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: mo is short for moment, a second

explanation.surface: A vineyard worker has a second new wine press installed outdoors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'new' rearranges PRESS GOING, which goes 'outside' MO. 'Grapevine' is the rumour mill, not a vine.
explanation.definitionFit: Hearing something on the grapevine means hearing rumour, so one who spreads rumour cultivates it.

clue.text: Artist stopping the rot with great speed

indicators.note: stopping means plugging a gap, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: rot meaning nonsense is bosh
c is the symbol for the speed of light, the greatest speed

explanation.surface: A painter quickly halts the decay.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the rot' is nonsense, not decay; C is the speed of light.
explanation.definitionFit: Hieronymus Bosch was a Dutch painter, an example of an artist.

clue.text: Soviet official, right to arrest one's son

indicators.note: to arrest is to stop or hold, so the comma holds the letters inside

parts.note: the printed punctuation mark itself is read as the word comma
one is I, so one's (one is) gives IS

explanation.surface: A Soviet officer has a right to detain somebody's son.
explanation.walkthrough: The comma after 'official' is part of the wordplay: COMMA + R holds ISS, giving COMM-ISS-A-R.
explanation.definitionFit: A commissar was a Communist Party official in the Soviet Union.

clue.text: A singer up to something

parts.note: a songbird such as a tit counts as a singer in crosswords

explanation.surface: A vocalist is plotting mischief.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Singer' suggests a human vocalist, but it is the small songbird.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone at it is busy with mischief, idiomatically the same as being up to something.

clue.text: In time I scrap publication, causing mixed feelings

indicators.note: the word scrap goes in between the letters for time and I

parts.note: a rag is a scrap of cloth
a comic is a magazine, a publication

explanation.surface: A writer dumps a magazine just in time, with mixed emotions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' governs the pair 'time I', so the scrap sits between those two letters; the order reads oddly against the clue but is the setter's intended split.
explanation.definitionFit: Something tragicomic mixes tragedy and comedy, so it causes mixed feelings of sorrow and laughter.

clue.text: Mini's re-designed new yet eye catching point

indicators.note: catching means taking in, so the letters hold another piece
redesigned means remade, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: N is north, a compass point

explanation.surface: A redesigned Mini car is new and eye-catching.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mini' looks like the car but is the adjective small. 're-designed' scrambles NEW YET EYE, which is 'catching' N.
explanation.definitionFit: Teeny-weeny is a childish word for tiny, so it means mini.

clue.text: Championship, one that provides seeds free entry

parts.note: an Open is a championship anyone may enter, as in golf or tennis
sesame is a plant grown for its seeds

explanation.surface: A tournament gives its seeded players a pass in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Seeds' suggests seeded tennis players, but it means plant seeds.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Ali Baba tale the magic phrase opens the cave, so it now names any easy means of entry.

clue.text: Parking fine rate

parts.note: P is the standard abbreviation for parking, as on road signs
ace is slang for excellent or fine

explanation.surface: A parking penalty is charged at a set rate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Parking fine' reads as a penalty notice; split it into P and ACE.
explanation.definitionFit: Pace and rate both mean speed of movement or progress, a straightforward synonym.

clue.text: School trust producing little feedback perhaps

parts.note: a high school, so high can stand for school
fidelity is faithfulness or trust

explanation.surface: A school's trust is getting little response from parents.
explanation.walkthrough: Feedback in audio is unwanted noise; equipment of the kind named reproduces sound faithfully, with little such distortion.
explanation.definitionFit: Hi-fi audio reproduces sound accurately, so it gives little unwanted feedback or distortion.

clue.text: To which son's praise may turn?

definitions.text: To which son's praise may turn?

indicators.note: turn means change into something else, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: the letters of son's count, including the S

explanation.surface: A rueful question about how a child's compliments can sour into insults.
explanation.walkthrough: 'may turn' rearranges SON'S PRAISE, and the whole clue is also the definition: praise turned sour becomes slander.
explanation.definitionFit: Aspersions are damaging remarks, so praise turning into them is the reverse of a compliment.

clue.text: The one playing keyboard most likely to be in a band?

definitions.text: The one playing keyboard most likely to be in a band?

parts.words: The one playing keyboard most likely to be in a band?
parts.note: reads as a musician in a group, but means the digit on a pianist's hand that usually wears a wedding band

explanation.walkthrough: 'band' suggests a pop group with a keyboard player; it is the ring worn on the fourth finger.
explanation.definitionFit: The fourth finger of the left hand is the one that traditionally wears a wedding ring.

clue.text: Page in Times has upset colleagues on board

indicators.note: the letter for page goes inside the rearranged letters
upset means knocked over and jumbled, so the words Times and has are rearranged

explanation.surface: A page in a newspaper has annoyed fellow workers on a committee.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Times' reads as the newspaper and 'on board' as a committee, but the answer's colleagues are fellow sailors.
explanation.definitionFit: Shipmates are fellow sailors, colleagues aboard the same vessel.

clue.text: Doctor who cut old dose excessively to ward off evil?

indicators.note: to doctor something is to tamper with it, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: to OD is to overdose, take a dose to excess

explanation.surface: A TV time-traveller cuts an old remedy with an overdose to keep evil away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Doctor who' suggests the TV series, but 'Doctor' is the anagram signal for WHO CUT O OD.
explanation.definitionFit: People say the phrase or tap wood superstitiously to avert bad luck.

clue.text: WC Fields's last English release

parts.note: a WC (water closet) is a loo, British for toilet

indicators.note: last asks for the final letter of Fields

explanation.surface: The comedian W.C. Fields's final English film is out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'WC Fields' reads as the American comedian, but split it: WC is the toilet, and Fields gives its last letter S.
explanation.definitionFit: To loose something is to set it free, so loose and release are verb synonyms.

clue.text: To encourage this face is obvious embarrassment

definitions.meaning: to urge someone on to do something
having the answer on your face is the idiom for being visibly embarrassed

explanation.walkthrough: The second half is a fill-in-the-blank: put the answer before 'face' to get the idiom for public embarrassment.
explanation.definitionFit: To egg someone on is to urge or encourage them; with face added it gives the idiom for looking foolish.

clue.text: From this country, drops in to collect a foreigner

parts.note: for a British paper, this country is the UK
raindrops, so drops gives rain

indicators.note: the word in collects, i.e. takes inside, the letter a

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Raindrops fall on a visitor from Britain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'This country' means Britain from the British paper's viewpoint, not the country the answer comes from; 'to collect' is the container signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A Ukrainian is a national of Ukraine, a foreigner from a British point of view.

clue.text: German writer penning long, terrifying story

indicators.note: penning means enclosing, as in a pen, so one word goes inside another

parts.note: Friedrich Schiller was a German poet and playwright
to long for something is to pine for it

explanation.surface: A German author writes a long, frightening tale.
explanation.walkthrough: 'penning' looks like writing, fitting a German author, but it means enclosing, as in a sheep pen.
explanation.definitionFit: A spine-chiller is a story frightening enough to send shivers down your back.

clue.text: Prompt payment before a last piece of work

parts.note: COD, cash on delivery, means payment made the moment goods arrive

explanation.surface: Someone is paid promptly before a final job.
explanation.walkthrough: COD is cash on delivery.
explanation.definitionFit: A coda is a closing passage concluding a piece of music or literature.

clue.text: Sky to remain endlessly blue

indicators.note: to sky a ball is to hit it high, so in a down clue the letters go up, reading in reverse
endlessly means the word loses its final letter

parts.note: to dwell is to remain or linger

explanation.surface: The sky stays a bit blue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sky' is not the heavens but the cricket verb for hitting the ball high: DWEL (DWELL less its last L, from 'endlessly') goes upward.
explanation.definitionFit: Blue, of jokes or films, means smutty or lewd.

clue.text: Excess pay grocer keeps back

indicators.note: back means the letters are read in reverse
the words pay grocer keep the letters inside them

explanation.surface: A shopkeeper withholds extra wages.
explanation.walkthrough: 'keeps' points to YGRO inside 'pay grocer'; 'back' turns it round.
explanation.definitionFit: An orgy is a bout of excessive indulgence, so excess stands for it.

clue.text: Pro cross when a leg's broken in racing

parts.note: pro means in favour of, i.e. for

indicators.note: the hybrid animal's letters are broken open with others inserted

parts.note: a mule is a cross between a horse and a donkey
in cricket, the leg side is also called the on side, so leg gives ON

explanation.surface: A professional is angry when he breaks a leg in a race.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cross' wants to mean angry, but it is the hybrid MULE, broken open by A and ON. Cricket's leg side is also called the on side.
explanation.definitionFit: Formula One is the top class of motor racing, an example of racing.

clue.text: One bound to land ride waves to audience

indicators.note: to an audience means as heard, so the word is the one that sounds alike

parts.note: to surf is to ride waves on a board

explanation.surface: Someone tied to the shore rides the waves for spectators.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to audience' signals a homophone: SURF sounds like the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A medieval serf was bound by law to work his lord's land.

clue.text: Dope and meals paid for prompt

parts.note: a dope is a fool or idiot
board is meals provided for payment, as in board and lodging

explanation.surface: A fool gets free meals on the spur of the moment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'prompt' looks like an adjective, but it is a noun: an idiot board is a cue card held up for TV presenters.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiot board is a large card showing a presenter their lines, a kind of prompt.
